# Why small teams ship faster

Most people assume that adding people makes a project faster. In practice, the opposite is
often true. Every new person adds communication paths, and each path is a place where context
gets lost. A team of three has three paths. A team of ten has forty-five.

Small teams avoid most of this. Everyone knows the whole system, decisions happen in a single
conversation, and nobody waits for a meeting to find out what changed. The cost of coordination
stays close to zero, so almost all of the effort goes into the work itself.

That does not mean small teams should stay small forever. It means that growth should be a
deliberate trade. Before adding someone, ask what coordination cost they bring, and whether the
extra hands are worth the extra conversations. If the answer is not obvious, wait.

There are three habits that help any team stay fast as it grows. First, write decisions down in
one place, so the reasoning outlives the meeting. Second, give every piece of work exactly one
owner, so there is never a question about who decides. Third, keep the unit of delivery small:
ship something every few days, not every few months, so mistakes are cheap and feedback is quick.

None of these habits are exotic. They work because they reduce the number of things a person has
to hold in their head. A fast team is not one that works harder. It is one that wastes less
effort on keeping everyone aligned, and spends the difference on building the thing that matters.

The practical takeaway is simple. Measure your team by how quickly an idea becomes something a
customer can use, not by how busy everyone looks. If that number is getting worse as you add
people, the problem is rarely effort. It is almost always coordination.
